The USS Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group has reportedly departed the US naval facility at Yokosuka, Japan, continuing its deployment toward the US Central Command area of responsibility amid heightened tensions with Iran.

The formation includes the Wasp-class amphibious assault ship USS Makin Island and two San Antonio-class amphibious transport docks, USS Anchorage and USS John P. Murtha. All three vessels were reportedly photographed departing Yokosuka minutes ago as the group continued its journey toward the CENTCOM region.

An amphibious ready group provides the US military with flexible capabilities for deploying Marines, conducting helicopter and landing operations, and responding to regional contingencies. Its movement toward the Middle East could strengthen Washington’s military options, although the deployment alone does not establish that offensive operations against Iran are planned.

lhd-8.tx:
The US Navy's Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group has left Yokosuka and is heading to CENTCOM. This is not a routine rotation. This is a reinforcement of a failing war. The US is sending a 2,200-Marine amphibious force with F-35B stealth fighters into a theater where its drones are being captured and its aircraft are squawking emergency codes.

🚢 The Force: Ships and Capabilities

The group is composed of three ships and an embarked Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU).

· USS Makin Island (LHD 8): The flagship. A Wasp-class amphibious assault ship. It is a light aircraft carrier in all but name. Its flight deck can accommodate the F-35B Lightning II stealth fighter, giving the group a fifth-generation strike capability. It can carry a mix of helicopters, MV-22 Ospreys, and up to 20 F-35Bs.
· USS Anchorage (LPD 23) and USS John P. Murtha (LPD 26): San Antonio-class amphibious transport docks. These ships carry the Marines, their vehicles, and their equipment. They are the delivery mechanism for a forced entry or a reinforced evacuation.

The embarked force is the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit (13th MEU). This is a Marine Air-Ground Task Force (MAGTF), meaning it is a self-sustaining combined-arms team with its own aviation, ground combat, and logistics elements. It brings:

◾A full squadron of F-35B Lightning II aircraft (VMFA-211), providing stealth strikes and close air support.
◾ Stealth strikes, vertical assault, maritime interdiction, and precision fires capability.
◾ Visit, Board, Search, and Seizure (VBSS) teams for maritime interdiction operations.

🎯 The Mission: Reinforcing a Losing War

This deployment is not a show of strength. It is a reaction to weakness. The US is sending this force to a theater where its existing posture has been degraded.

◾ The drone attrition: The US has lost 56 MQ-9 Reapers (each ~$30 million) and had six MQM-170 drones captured intact by Iranian electronic warfare over Qeshm Island.
◾The aircraft in distress: Two US military aircraft, including a CMV-22B Osprey (the carrier's logistics lifeline), recently squawked 7700 (emergency) in the same window.
◾The ground collapse: The Saudi-led coalition, a US partner, is bombing its own allies and losing commanders (Badr Al-Harbi in the Kahub range, Fares Al-Shammari in Al-Jawf).
◾The political collapse: The US midterms saw the Democratic Party win both chambers. Vice President JD Vance admitted the war lost the election.

The Makin Island ARG is being sent to plug a hole. It is a crisis response force deployed to a crisis that the US is losing.

🔗 The Deeper Layer: The Meat Grinder and the Chokepoints

This deployment is a node in the same architecture that is grinding Ukraine and Iran. It is the military enforcement arm of a financial system that needs to control the world's chokepoints.

◾The Chokepoints: The force is heading to a region where the Strait of Hormuz is contested. The Iranian Army has stated the strait will only reopen when the US accepts Iran's seven conditions. The US Navy has been unable to open it. This amphibious group is a desperate attempt to change the facts on the water.
◾ The Financial Architecture: The US is deploying this force while its own political system reels from a war that cost $47 billion and failed to achieve its objectives. The same financial oligarchy that funds the US military is now renegotiating the receipts, with Trump's model being equity in Ukrainian minerals and a bail-in directive in Europe.

The Bill

The USS Makin Island, USS Anchorage, and USS John P. Murtha. The 13th MEU with its F-35Bs. 2,200 Marines heading to a theater where the US has lost 56 Reapers, six MQM-170s, and two aircraft squawked 7700.

This is not a strategy. It is a reinforcement of a failure. The US is sending its most capable amphibious force into a conflict where its drones are being harvested and its proxies are collapsing. cvn-73.t: The US military is conducting nightly missions over the Strait of Hormuz as American forces work to enforce a blockade on Iranian ports along the waterway and…
cvn-73.tx:
The US military is conducting nightly missions over the Strait of Hormuz as American forces work to enforce a blockade on Iranian ports along the waterway and protect commercial vessels at risk of being struck by Iranian projectiles.
The airspace over the waterway is only about 20 miles wide but is full of aerial objects, giving fighter jet pilots a small window to react to any projectiles launched from Iran’s coast.
Rear Adm. Jeffrey Heames, who commands the USS George Washington Carrier Strike Group, said that US forces have been reliably striking down threats to commercial shipping in the region.
“If there’s a threat that’s launched against those vessels, whether it’s an anti-ship cruise missile or a drone, those aircraft will go in and intercept it and shoot it down in a very short amount of time,”
According to US Central Command (CENTCOM), the protection provided by the US Navy has allowed Gulf partners to export over 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since the summer. Over the past six months, more than 3,000 commercial vessels have successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz without incident.
US military leaders say that their forces can maintain the blockade and protect the strait for as long as is needed.

By GOLDIE KATZ
OCTOBER 31, 2026 02:05

qt.t:
I just found the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier (CVN-71) on Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, 04/11/2026.

It is currently sailing westwards in the South China Sea, headed for the Strait of Malacca, to proceed towards the Middle East.

Coordinates: 6.02843, 108.47420

cvn-77.tx:
This Sentinel-2 image clearly shows the full carrier strike group centered on the USS Theodore Roosevelt.

The group consists of the Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, three Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, and a Ticonderoga-class cruiser, notably, it is also accompanied by a Seahawk MUSV, though the latter is not visible in this image.

The three destroyers are the USS Paul Hamilton, the USS Decatur, and the USS Carl M. Levin, while the cruiser is the USS Chosin; the entire strike group, comprising five primary vessels, is headed toward the Middle East.

It remains unclear whether it will serve as an additional carrier force or replace the USS George H.W. Bush, in any case, I expect it to arrive in the CENTCOM area of responsibility in about ten days, around the middle of November.

cvn-76.t: Laura Montero never thought her fun cruise to Mexico would end on a U.S. naval carrier surrounded by 3,000 sailors... The 14-year-old owes her life to the men…
cvn-76.tx:
Laura Montero never thought her fun cruise to Mexico would end on a U.S. naval carrier surrounded by 3,000 sailors...

The 14-year-old owes her life to the men and women of the USS Ronald Reagan, one of the largest aircraft carriers in the Navy, who saved her in a mission worthy of Hollywood script.

. . . 

In December 2007, 14-year-old Laura Montero from Albion, Illinois, was vacationing with her family on the Dawn Princess cruise ship off the coast of Baja California, Mexico, when she suddenly fell violently ill. Her appendix ruptured, presenting a life-threatening medical emergency while the ship was hundreds of miles out at sea and far from standard civilian surgical care.

With the cruise ship unable to reach land quickly enough, a distress call was answered by the nearby nuclear-powered U.S. Navy aircraft carrier USS Ronald Reagan, which was returning from a training tour. The massive warship altered its course and raced through the night. At around 5:00 a.m., a helicopter launched from the carrier to close the final 175-mile gap. Because there was no space to land on the cruise liner, a Navy medic was lowered onto the deck in a basket to retrieve Laura, placing her on an antibiotic drip before hoisting her into the aircraft.

Brought safely aboard the USS Ronald Reagan, Laura underwent a successful emergency appendectomy performed by the ship’s surgeon just hours later. Her mother was later flown out to reunite with her on the carrier, and Laura completed her journey back to mainland San Diego aboard the warship, fully recovering from the ordeal thanks to the extraordinary coordinated rescue.

Because the USS Ronald Reagan was a classified military warship, special diplomatic and naval clearance had to be swiftly coordinated to allow a civilian cruise passenger onto a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, marking an exceptionally rare instance of the U.S. Navy executing such a medical evacuation.

al-udeid.t: Explosions on Qeshm Island and near Bandar Lengeh overnight, and in the SAME hours Qatar, Pakistan and China are carrying messages between Tehran and Washingto…
al-udeid.tx:
Explosions on Qeshm Island and near Bandar Lengeh overnight, and in the SAME hours Qatar, Pakistan and China are carrying messages between Tehran and Washington... 🔴

So what?

US officials call it "limited" and "defensive". An IRGC missile went up from Qeshm at a US aircraft over the Strait of Hormuz Monday night, the jet destroyed the launcher, and Iran says it has now downed its 55th MQ-9 Reaper. Both capitals walk away with a story they can sell at home.

But WHY now?

Because Americans vote TODAY. Trump says "We had a war with Iran. We won", says there has been no fighting "for months", and told reporters he will NOT strike Iran after the midterms. A big strike wrecks that message the day before the vote, and doing nothing looks weak with Brent at $105 and drones falling out of the sky. A small "defensive" hit on ONE launcher is the only option that serves both needs.

And this was a PROBING strike. Qeshm is the largest island in the Strait, the IRGC's forward position on the world's most important oil lane, with Bandar Lengeh right across on the mainland. Hit it small and you learn how fast the IRGC detects, how its air defence reacts, whether Tehran answers or absorbs, and what it says through the mediators the next morning. Iran runs the same test in reverse with every Reaper it claims, measuring how much Washington will swallow before it answers.

Both sides are climbing the escalation ladder ONE rung at a time, each careful to stop below the rung that forces the other into full war.

And none of the mediators is neutral. Qatar hosts Al Udeid, the largest US base in the region, and China has been the main buyer of Iranian oil, so every strike gets priced into the next message they carry.

Washington's danger is drift: limited strikes become routine, each one invites a bigger IRGC answer, and ONE dead aircrew or ONE tanker hit in Hormuz pushes Trump up the ladder whether he wants it or not. For Tehran, the Reaper count proves it can bleed the US cheaply, and also tempts the IRGC to keep pushing past the point where the next rung stops being optional...

Trump's own line, no strikes after the midterms, is now on the record. If Qeshm or Bandar Lengeh is hit again before the end of November, the talks are cover for a slow return to the war.

al-udeid.t: 🇮🇷|Araghchi: Some Regional Countries Encouraged the American Attack. He Did Not Name Them. The Bases Name Them. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi stated: "Unfort…
al-udeid.tx:
🇮🇷|Araghchi: Some Regional Countries Encouraged the American Attack. He Did Not Name Them. The Bases Name Them.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi stated: "Unfortunately, I must say that some regional countries encouraged the Americans to attack Iran, and I hope they too have learned their lessons. The best approach is to convince their friends in America that a new war should not begin. Regional countries should be cautious that a new war does not take shape."

"Some regional countries" is diplomatic cover for a file that is not classified. Identify them by their coordinates.

Qatar: Al Udeid Air Base at 25.12°N 51.32°E, CENTCOM forward headquarters, the largest US installation in the region. The aircraft that flew against Iran launched from or were supported by Al Udeid.

Bahrain: Naval Support Activity Bahrain at 26.21°N 50.61°E, home of the US Fifth Fleet. The fleet that enforced the naval blockade on Iranian ports operates from Bahraini water.

Kuwait: Camp Arifjan at 28.90°N 48.19°E and Ali Al Salem Air Base at 29.35°N 47.52°E, the logistics spine for US ground and air forces in the theater.

Saudi Arabia: Prince Sultan Air Base at 24.06°N 47.58°E, the US air hub for the central region, plus overflight corridors and the Saudi air defense network integrated with US systems.

The UAE: Al Dhafra Air Base at 24.25°N 54.55°E, the F-35 and ISR hub, plus Jebel Ali port, the largest US military logistics node in the Gulf.

Jordan: Muwaffaq Salti Air Base at 31.83°N 36.82°E, the launch point for the daily drone incursions over Iraqi airspace into the Iranian approach.

Every one of those countries is a host. Every one of them encouraged the attack by providing the ground, the runway, the fuel, the radar, and the political cover. Araghchi's "some regional countries" is a list of six capitals. The coordinates are the names.

"I hope they too have learned their lessons" is not a hope. It is an accounting.

The lesson was delivered. 274 US military facilities damaged across seven countries. The damage is not confined to American property. The host states absorbed the strikes on their soil, the closure of their airports, the collapse of their insurance markets, and the loss of their reputations as safe places to invest.

More than 7,800 flights cancelled or grounded across Saudi Arabia between 8 and 25 October. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport shut for more than a week. 86 per cent of its scheduled departures affected. Lufthansa, Air India, KLM, British Airways, Cathay Pacific, Etihad, Flydubai, and Oman Air suspended or extended cancellations. The Future Investment Initiative, the kingdom's flagship investment conference postponed to 2027.

That is the lesson. The host states learned that renting their soil to Washington converts their infrastructure into targets. Araghchi is reminding them.

The hidden layer: the "friends in America" line is the actual instruction.

Araghchi said: "The best approach is to convince their friends in America that a new war should not begin."

That is Tehran telling the Gulf capitals to spend their lobbying budgets on preventing the next war, not on supporting it. The Gulf states have spent decades buying influence in Washington through the sovereign wealth funds, the weapons contracts, the real estate partnerships, the think tanks, and the lobbying firms. Araghchi is telling them to use that influence to restrain the White House instead of encouraging it.

It is also a warning. If the Gulf states fail to restrain Washington, and a new war begins, the response will reach their soil again. The Zero Hour list has not been withdrawn. The target bank has been updated. The IRGC spokesperson announced new targets and new geographic areas from Kerman. Araghchi's caution is the diplomatic form of that military statement.

Fresh satellite imagery reportedly shows no significant reduction in the U.S. aircraft presence at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, with roughly 27 aircraft still visible.

Not proof that a strike isn’t coming — but certainly an indicator worth watching.

al-dhafra.t: 🇴🇲🇦🇪|Oman and Abu Dhabi: Two US Military Aircraft Squawked 7700 in the Same Window. The US Navy's Carrier Logistics Aircraft Is in Trouble. A US Navy CMV-22B O…
al-dhafra.tx:
🇴🇲🇦🇪|Oman and Abu Dhabi: Two US Military Aircraft Squawked 7700 in the Same Window. The US Navy's Carrier Logistics Aircraft Is in Trouble.

A US Navy CMV-22B Osprey transmitted emergency squawk 7700 while flying along the southern coast of Oman on 6 November 2026. The code signals an in-flight emergency requiring immediate landing.

In the same window, a second US military aircraft squawked 7700 near Abu Dhabi, at around 17,000 feet.

The Osprey Is Not a Fighter. It Is the Carrier's Lifeline.

The CMV-22B is the Navy's carrier onboard delivery platform. It moves personnel, cargo, and essential equipment between coastal bases and aircraft carriers.

It is the aircraft that carries the F-35 engine modules, the mail, the specialists, and the priority spares that keep a carrier strike group operating. Without the Osprey, the carrier is tethered to a port.

A CMV-22B in distress is not a tactical loss. It is a logistics failure for the carrier group it serves.

The Attack Claim Is Unconfirmed. Report It as Such.

Tasnim reported that the aircraft came under attack off the coast of Oman. The claim is unconfirmed. No US Central Command statement has confirmed an attack.

Signal, Not noise!

muwaffaq-salti.t: A major @WSJ investigation documents the extensive damage Iranian missile and drone attacks have inflicted on US military bases across the Middle East, and how…
muwaffaq-salti.tx:
A major @WSJ investigation documents the extensive damage Iranian missile and drone attacks have inflicted on US military bases across the Middle East, and how Iran's targeting has evolved over the course of the war.

The Pentagon privately estimates at least $5 billion in damage to US bases, potentially as much as $15 billion. That's on top of $47.1 billion in other war costs through October 16. More than 20 US servicemembers have been killed in war-related activity, with over 400 wounded before the July ceasefire collapsed, when the Pentagon stopped publishing war-specific casualty figures.

In the first two weeks alone, at least 119 buildings across 13 installations were damaged, particularly in Kuwait. Iran also struck radar, missile-defense, and communications infrastructure. The US largely evacuated several bases, including its Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain and major installations in Kuwait.

Perhaps most significant is how Iranian attacks evolved. Following the July ceasefire collapse, Iran increasingly struck bases farther from its borders, particularly in Jordan, while hitting smaller, more specific targets, including buildings housing American troops. A July 17 strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan killed three US servicemembers and damaged at least 19 buildings where troops sleep.

The WSJ's satellite analysis suggests growing Iranian targeting precision and an ability to adapt its operations despite months of US and Israeli strikes. The Pentagon has been forced to disperse personnel, reconsider its regional basing posture, and weigh relocating installations farther from Iran.

All of this stands in striking contrast to repeated public claims by Trump administration officials that Iran's missile capabilities had been effectively destroyed. In March, Hegseth declared Iran's ballistic missile production capacity functionally defeated. In April, Trump said its missiles were nearly exhausted. In July, days after the deadly Jordan strike, Hegseth described Iran as "completely overmatched and crushed" and "combat ineffective."

Yet Iran continued striking US installations, inflicting casualties and billions in damage.

The broader strategic implication is that degrading Iran's military capabilities has not eliminated its ability to impose substantial costs on the US regional military presence.

The war has exposed the vulnerability of America's large, fixed bases to Iranian missiles and drones, raising difficult questions for the US about the sustainability of its posture in the Middle East and the consequences of another round of escalation.

Commodities were already ahead of both before Hormuz - it just widened the gap.

diego-garcia.tx:
A lot of smart people believe that the war will have one of two outcomes: either there will be an agreement, or a perpetual state of on/off. 

But I disagree. The chances of both of these events are very small. The most likely outcome is that the US leaves. Whether it will empty its magazine before leaving is tbd. 

A) Donald Trump can’t offer anything to Iran that would be considered better than the JCPOA by both sides. If it’s more favorable to Iran than the JCPOA, it will not be acceptable by the American side. If it’s less favorable to Iran than the JCPOA, while Iran’s advantages have materially increased, it won’t be acceptable for Iranians. 

B) The US doesn’t have the material and the logistical capability to maintain a permanent blockade of Iran or presence close enough to project force regularly. 

The US does not have the logistical capabilities for aircraft carriers. Currently they’re being provisioned from Diego Garcia and the Far East. 

Iran isn’t going to capitulate. The only option left is for the US to leave.

akrotiri.tx:
As negotiations fail, the Islamic Republic is threatening Europe with missile attacks.

The Islamic Republic has released a harrowing video threatening Europe with military retaliation and warning that European countries could face missile attacks.

The cinematic video was published by Iran in Arabic, an Arabic-language account that presents itself as the Islamic Republic’s voice in the Arab world, and framed as a “dangerous warning” from the regime’s armed forces.

Set across European streets, subway stations and cafés, it shows a regime figure appearing on public screens while crowds carry signs reading “NO MORE BLOOD,” “NO MORE AGGRESSION” and “NO MORE LIES.”

The message attempts to address Europeans directly while implying that their cities and civilians could face consequences if their governments continue supporting American and Israeli military action.

This was not an isolated propaganda release.

On the same day, Kayhan, which is closely connected to the Supreme Leader’s circle, warned that American and NATO facilities “in the heart of Europe” could be attacked. It named military sites in Cyprus, Greece, Romania, Albania, Italy and Britain.

Hamshahri simultaneously published a map marking military sites across nine European countries under the threatening headline “We’ll see what happens.”

Regime commanders have also declared that earlier geographic limits no longer apply. They now claim missile ranges of between 4,000 and 5,000 kilometres, placing much of Europe within their threatened strike zone.

The Islamic Republic has already moved beyond propaganda:

▪️ A drone struck RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus during the wider conflict.

▪️ The regime attempted long-range missile strikes against the joint American-British base at Diego Garcia.

▪️ Iranian missiles travelling westward were intercepted over Turkish territory.

▪️ European intelligence services have uncovered IRGC-linked assassination, arson, surveillance and sabotage operations across the continent.

▪️ British authorities charged two men over activity near RAF Fairford that the British government assessed was highly likely coordinated from Iran and almost certainly directed by the IRGC.

The pattern combines overt military threats with deniable covert action. Regime media publishes maps and videos. Commanders expand the declared target zone. IRGC networks use criminal proxies and operatives to test European security from within.

The timing is significant. Negotiations have failed to produce an agreement, the Islamic Republic has rejected the latest American response and military reinforcements are moving into the region.

The regime is now trying to frighten Europe away from supporting the next campaign by making European governments believe that their bases, infrastructure and populations could become targets.

This is not diplomacy from a government seeking coexistence. It is coercion from a regime responding to failed negotiations by expanding its threats from the Persian Gulf to Europe itself.

It is the Space Force.

whiteman.tx:
Ask any American infantryman why he never lets an A-10 Warthog pilot pay for his own beer, and he will tell you about a day like December 2, 2010.

Sixteen soldiers from the 201st Engineer Battalion of the Kentucky Army National Guard were clearing a mountain road out of Kandahar, Afghanistan, when rocket-propelled grenades crippled their first four vehicles at once.

Heavy machine-gun fire poured down from fortified stone positions along the ridgeline, pinning the sixteen Americans in a kill zone with nowhere to retreat.

After forty minutes of brutal combat, Specialist Mauricio Arias and Sergeant Joseph Parker looked at their rifles and realized the platoon was down to its final magazine of ammunition.

Rather than wait to be overrun and executed, the sixteen soldiers prepared to fix bayonets and charge straight up the hill on foot.

Then two A-10 Warthogs from the 303rd Fighter Squadron dropped out of the sky.

In the lead cockpit sat Captain Tony Roe, callsign Crack. On his wing flew Captain John Tice, callsign Sapper, a former enlisted U.S. Army combat engineer who knew exactly what it felt like to be bleeding in the mud below.

Calling the platoon leader on the FM radio, Roe asked the soldiers to pop a smoke grenade and declared Emergency Close Air Support.

Why is that declaration so rare?

Because declaring Emergency Close Air Support means the pilot personally accepts full legal responsibility if a single round strikes friendly troops.

On his first pass, Roe squeezed the trigger of his thirty-millimeter cannon, but a digital elevation glitch in the targeting computer sent the shells high over the ridge.

Without wasting ten seconds, Roe switched off the computer's elevation data, keyed in the altitude manually by hand, and dove back into the wall of machine-gun fire.

Flying low enough for the soldiers to read the numbers on his fuselage, Roe unleashed seven high-explosive rockets just forty meters from the American trench while Tice made six consecutive strafing passes with his thirty-millimeter Gatling gun.

To the sixteen men on the ground, that low tearing roar sounded like angels singing.

When the smoke cleared, thirty-two enemy fighters were dead, and every single American soldier walked out alive.

Nine years later, at Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri, Arias and Parker sat in the audience and stood with tears in their eyes to salute the two pilots as they received the Distinguished Flying Cross.

To a politician, the A-10 is an old budget line, but to an infantryman on his last magazine, that ugly gray jet is a brother coming down from heaven.

fort-bragg.tx:
🚨 BREAKING: Another leaker CAUGHT and this one had TOP SECRET clearance.

The FBI just arrested James Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, NC - a former Fort Bragg contractor who worked security at the U.S. Army Special Operations Command.

Think about that. This guy held a TOP SECRET clearance with SCI access. One of the highest clearances in the country. And what did he allegedly do with it?

According to the DOJ indictment unsealed Tuesday, he photographed classified military operation videos and photos and just POSTED THEM ON SOCIAL MEDIA. 🤯

Not to a journalist. Not by accident. He allegedly took classified footage of actual military operations and uploaded it where anyone could see it. Then other users spread it to a second site.

And when it started going viral, he panicked. He allegedly messaged someone begging them to take it down, saying he was "trying to do some damage control."

Too late.

When FBI Charlotte searched his home, they reportedly found MORE - a classified award write-up with additional national defense info still sitting at his house, AND a missing night vision goggle system that belonged to a Special Operations unit. Stolen government property.

This is exactly why we can't be soft on leakers. This is Special Operations. These are the guys who do the missions we never hear about. Their operations, their identities, their equipment - all of it is classified for a reason. To keep them alive.

You leak that for clout on social media? You are a traitor to every operator who trusts that system.

Thank GOD he was caught. The DOJ is charging him with unlawfully transmitting and retaining national defense information and theft of government property.

NO MERCY FOR LEAKERS AND TRAITORS. Lock him up. 🇺🇸

pearl-harbor.tx:
Easy Company radioman George Luz is portrayed by Rick Gomez in "Band of Brothers". George Luz was born in Fall River, Massachusetts in 1921 and was one of ten children. During the Great Depression, he helped earn money for his family by working as a shoe shine boy, and he would also carry ice up several flights of stairs to fill people's ice boxes. He dropped out of school his junior year so that he could help his family survive financially. After Pearl Harbor, he felt the call to enlist and did so in August 1942. He volunteered for the paratroopers because they were the best of the best, and like many of the men, he liked the extra pay.

George Luz trained at Camp Toccoa, Georgia as part of Easy Company, 2nd Battalion, 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment, 101st Airborne Division under the strict command of Captain Herbert Sobel, who is portrayed by actor David Schwimmer in "Band of Brothers". Like in the series, George Luz became known for his sense of humor and his skill at imitation, which is highlighted in "Band of Brothers" when he mimics Major Oliver Horton's voice and convinces Captain Sobel to cut a barbed-wire fence, causing a farmer's cows to get out. George fought with Easy Company in Normandy, Holland, and at Bastogne during the Battle of the Bulge, and he remained relatively uninjured throughout his time in WWII.

After the war, George went home to Rhode Island where he worked a variety of jobs before returning to the textile industry, which he had been employed in when he enlisted. He struck up a romance with a woman named Delvina Rogers, or Del as he called her, who was the younger sister of his neighborhood friend, Tony. George and Delvina married in 1948 and had three children. Similar to how he was viewed when he was part of Easy Company, George was beloved in his Rhode Island community and had many friends. After working in the textile industry, he became a machine mechanic. In the 1970s, he decided to go back to school to earn his GED to make up for never having been able to graduate high school during the Great Depression.

George and his wife attended the yearly Easy Company reunions. Dick Winters described George Luz as being "one of the pillars of Easy Company." To my knowledge, there isn't a single member of Easy Company, who when talking about George Luz, didn't speak highly of him. Of his time with Easy Company, George stated, "It was the best three years of my life." #bandofbrothers #ww2 #easycompay #WWII

yokosuka.t: September 12, 2001. Armed US sailors lock down the main gate of Yokosuka Naval Base and brace for another attack. Within hours, a crowd of Japanese citizens be…
yokosuka.tx:
September 12, 2001. Armed US sailors lock down the main gate of Yokosuka Naval Base and brace for another attack.

Within hours, a crowd of Japanese citizens begins walking toward the concrete barriers.

The commander of the base was a 48 year old US Navy Captain. His name was Robert Francois.

Hours earlier, on the night of September 11 in Japan, four hijacked planes had struck New York, the Pentagon, and Pennsylvania. Half a world away, the 20,000 Americans stationed at Yokosuka, home of the US Seventh Fleet, were cut off from home. Phone lines to the United States were jammed. Young sailors stood watch in full combat gear behind steel barricades, terrified for their families and expecting further strikes.

They felt completely alone.

Then the sun came up over Tokyo Bay.

One by one, residents from the city of Yokosuka walked up to the armed guards at the main gate. An elderly woman bowed in silence and placed a bouquet of white chrysanthemums on the pavement.

Not a word.

Then came schoolchildren carrying strings of 1,000 folded paper cranes.

By afternoon, the security barrier was buried under a wall of fresh flowers, candles, American flags, and handwritten notes. On scraps of paper, Japanese neighbors had written in careful English: "We cry with you" and "America, stay strong."

Here's where it gets even more moving. Ten days later, on September 21, when the aircraft carrier USS Kitty Hawk departed Yokosuka, thousands of Japanese citizens and Maritime Self Defense Force sailors lined the harbor waving American flags to see the crew off.

Captain Robert Francois retired from the Navy in 2003 after 30 years of service. Ten years after 9/11, when the March 2011 tsunami devastated northern Japan, the Seventh Fleet sailed straight from Yokosuka to launch Operation Tomodachi, rescuing thousands of Japanese families.

On the darkest morning in modern American history, a city that once fought the US Navy made sure its sailors never cried alone.

yokosuka.tx:
My wife's aunt is a midwife. Last month, after 34 years, she retired.

Her hospital is near the U.S. Navy base in Yokosuka. In 34 years, she delivered 412 American babies.

At her retirement party, she gave a speech. Half of it was about American fathers.

"When I started," she said, "Japanese fathers waited in the hallway. Or at the office.

American fathers came into the room. They only ever leave for one reason."

Some of what she said:

"They pack a bag for themselves. Snacks. Chargers. A speaker. One had a playlist called BABY DAY. The baby did not care for it."

"They coach. 'Breathe, babe. You got this. Big push.' Like it's fourth and goal. The mothers tell them to be quiet. They get quieter. They never stop."

"They cry. The bigger the man, the louder. A Navy chief with a neck as wide as my waist cried so hard, I almost gave HIM the oxygen."

"I write the weight in grams. 3,290. The father does math on his phone, runs into the hallway, and announces it like a final score. 'SEVEN POUNDS, FOUR OUNCES!' Strangers clap. Thirty-four years, I still don't know what an ounce is."

"Every one of them introduces himself. 'Hey, buddy. I'm your dad.' As if the baby might ask for ID."

"They inspect the car seat for 40 minutes. Then they drive home at the speed of a bicycle with the hazard lights on."

Then she stopped smiling.

"And sometime in the first hour, every single one of them walks out to the hallway alone and calls his father.

Big men. Quiet men. Men who told me they hadn't spoken to their fathers in years.

They all call."

"In 2019, a young sailor called. It went to voicemail. He left a long message. 'Dad. It's a boy. He's got your ears. We named him after you.'

The next day, he called again. And the next.

On the fourth day, his wife told me. His father had died eight months before. His mother never cancelled the phone. She still pays for it, so she can hear his voice.

He called that number every day until they took the baby home."

She looked at the room for a long time.

"In 34 years, I learned one thing about American men.

The moment they become fathers, they become sons again."

When she sat down, nobody clapped for a while.

Then, one by one, the Japanese men in the room stood up and walked out to the hallway.

I was the third.

yokosuka.t: Every year, my wife's high school does an exchange with the U.S. Navy base in Yokosuka. Her students write letters to sailors. The sailors write back. Some of…
yokosuka.tx:
Every year, my wife's high school does an exchange with the U.S. Navy base in Yokosuka. Her students write letters to sailors. The sailors write back.

Some of this year's letters, spelling fixed:

"Dear Sailor, is it true you can eat breakfast at any time of day? Please answer honestly."

"Dear Sailor, what is the biggest wave you have seen? Bigger than our school?"

"Dear Sailor, my grandfather says American sailors helped his town after the tsunami. He says thank you. I am saying it for him, because his English is not good."

"Dear Sailor, do you miss your dog? I would miss my dog."

Then there was a girl who wrote only three lines.

"You are very far from home.
In Japan, when someone works hard, we say 'otsukaresama.'
Your mother cannot say it to you right now, so I will say it for her."

The sailor who got that letter is 19. From a small town in Ohio. His first time away from home.

He wrote back one page. My wife let me read it.

He said he'd been homesick for four months and hadn't told anybody. He said he read her letter three times, standing in the passageway.

Then he did something nobody expected.

He mailed her letter home to his mother.

Last week, an envelope arrived at my wife's school. Postmarked Ohio. Addressed to the girl.

Inside was a card.

"Thank you for saying it for me.
I've said it to his picture every night since he left.
I'm so glad somebody over there finally said it out loud."

yokosuka.t: September 9, 1942. A Japanese floatplane launches off the coast of Oregon to drop firebombs on the US mainland. Fifty five years later, that exact Oregon town…
yokosuka.tx:
September 9, 1942. A Japanese floatplane launches off the coast of Oregon to drop firebombs on the US mainland.

Fifty five years later, that exact Oregon town named him an honorary citizen.

His name was Nobuo Fujita.

At 30 years old, Warrant Officer Fujita became the only pilot in history to bomb the continental United States during wartime. Flying a tiny Yokosuka E14Y floatplane launched from the submarine I 25, he dropped two incendiary bombs over Wheeler Ridge near Brookings, Oregon. Rain soaked forests kept the flames small, and nobody was hurt.

Twenty years later, in 1962, the Junior Chamber of Commerce in Brookings came up with an unthinkable idea. They invited the man who bombed them to be the guest of honor at their Azalea Festival.

Fujita was terrified it was a trap.

Before boarding his flight to America, he packed his family's 400 year old samurai sword in his luggage. He promised himself that if the townspeople pelted him with rotten eggs or put him on trial as a war criminal, he would use the blade to take his own life in the traditional way.

It wasn't a trap.

Three thousand Americans lined the streets of Brookings to shake his hand and welcome him. Stunned by their grace, Fujita walked into the town hall and handed over his 400 year old family sword as a gift of peace.

Here's where it gets even deeper. Fujita never stopped paying the town back.

In 1985, he brought three students from Brookings to Japan at his own expense after his company went bankrupt. In the 1990s, when he heard Brookings was struggling to build a new public library, the elderly pilot mailed checks totaling 15,000 dollars from his modest savings.

In September 1997, Nobuo Fujita died of lung cancer in Japan at age 85. Days before he passed, Brookings made him an honorary citizen.

The following year, his daughter Yoriko flew to Oregon and buried a portion of his ashes at the exact bomb site in the forest, right beside a redwood seedling he had planted himself.

He flew to Oregon twice: once to burn their forest down, and once to plant a tree where his ashes now rest.

kadena.t: 🇯🇵 - A Japanese bomber landed on its belly at an American airfield. Then armed men climbed out. Their mission had only just begun. On the night of May 24–25, 1…
kadena.tx:
🇯🇵 - A Japanese bomber landed on its belly at an American airfield. Then armed men climbed out. Their mission had only just begun.

On the night of May 24–25, 1945, Japanese aircraft approached Okinawa, where American forces had captured airfields and put them to work against their former owners.

Among the attackers were Mitsubishi Ki-21 "Sally" bombers carrying an unusual cargo: commandos equipped with demolition charges, grenades, and small arms.

These were men of the Giretsu airborne raiding force.

Their targets were the American aircraft parked at Yontan and Kadena. Destroying them on the ground could weaken the fighter cover that was intercepting Japan’s kamikaze attacks.

There was no extraction plan. They were expected to land, destroy as much as possible, and fight on.

The operation began to unravel before most of the raiders reached their objectives. Aircraft turned back, failed to find their targets, or were shot down.

But one bomber got through.

It made a wheels-up landing at Yontan. Commandos emerged onto the American airfield.

Although drawn from airborne troops, they had not parachuted in. Their aircraft had delivered them directly into the target.

They attacked parked planes and fuel installations with grenades and incendiary charges. Aircraft burned. Fuel dumps containing roughly 70,000 gallons of gasoline went up in flames.

For hours, defenders hunted the raiders through the darkness. Confusion compounded the damage: the Marine Corps’ official account records Americans accidentally firing on their own men.

By the time the last attacker was killed, several American aircraft had been destroyed and many others damaged.

The raid had inflicted real damage, but it could not reverse the battle for Okinawa.

These men are sometimes called “kamikaze paratroopers.”

Share this overlooked chapter of the Pacific War, and follow @Vanguard_WW2 for more stories behind the familiar history.

kadena.t: My friend Makoto spent 28 years as a rescue diver with the Japan Coast Guard. He has pulled 140 people out of the sea. He says the number is wrong. In Septembe…
kadena.tx:
My friend Makoto spent 28 years as a rescue diver with the Japan Coast Guard.

He has pulled 140 people out of the sea.

He says the number is wrong.

In September 1984, Makoto was twelve years old. His father was a fisherman on a small island in Okinawa. They went out one morning in a calm sea. By afternoon, a typhoon had turned and come for them.

By dark, the boat was upside down.

Makoto and his father clung to the hull in water the color of a bruise. Waves as tall as houses. Rain so hard it hurt. His father had hit his head going over. He was bleeding. He was getting cold. He was getting quiet.

Makoto held onto him and screamed into a wind that took every word away.

Then there was a sound above the storm.

A helicopter. From Kadena, the American air base. Its searchlight came down through the rain like a hand reaching into the water.

And out of the open door, a man came down on a single thread of steel cable.

He swung in the wind like a bell. The rotor wash flattened the waves around them into a silver bowl. And he dropped into the black water right next to them, so close Makoto could see his eyes.

He was an Air Force pararescueman. A PJ. Twenty-six years old. His name was Cole.

Makoto was so terrified, he said the only thing that came into his head. In Japanese.

"Are you God?"

Cole didn't understand a word. But he understood the face.

He grinned, water pouring off his helmet.

"No, buddy. I'm from Oregon."

He grabbed Makoto by the life vest and pulled him close.

"Hey. Hey. Look at me. Not the waves. Me. The ocean's loud. I'm louder."

He clipped Makoto into the harness. He sent him up first. The boy rose out of the sea into the light, spinning, crying, looking down at his father and the man in the water getting smaller.

Then the crew chief shouted something into the radio.

The helicopter was nearly out of fuel. The storm had taken too long. They had to go. Now. Or no one would make it home.

There was no time to bring up two more.

In the water, Cole looked at the father. Bleeding. Half-conscious. Too weak to hold on alone.

He made a decision in about one second.

He tied the father's body to his own with a rope. Chest to chest. And he waved the helicopter away.

He stayed.

Makoto watched from the window as the helicopter turned. Below, in that black, heaving ocean, there was one tiny light. The strobe on Cole's shoulder. Blinking. Like a heartbeat.

Then the rain closed in. And it was gone.

Makoto pressed his face to the window and screamed for his father all the way back to the base. A crew member he never saw again held him the entire flight and didn't let go.

They refueled in nineteen minutes. They went back out into the typhoon.

For forty minutes, in the dark, in waves that broke over his head again and again, Cole held a stranger's father above the water.

He talked to him the entire time. The father didn't speak English. It didn't matter. Cole told him about Oregon. About his mom. About the river behind his house where he learned to swim. About how his son was going to be just fine. About how they were going to go home now. He kept saying it. "We're going home now. We're going home."

He sang to him when he ran out of things to say. Every song he knew. Badly. Into a typhoon.

When the searchlight found them again, the strobe was still blinking.

They came up together. Still tied.

Makoto's father lived.

Three days later, Cole came to the hospital in Naha. He was too big for the chair. He tried to say "konnichiwa" and got it wrong. He let Makoto try on his maroon beret. It covered his whole face.

Makoto's father, in the bed, took Cole's hand in both of his. He couldn't stop bowing. He tried to thank him through a nurse who spoke a little English.

Cole just shook his head.

"Sir. I don't leave people in the water. That's the whole job."

Before he left, Cole pulled something off his gear and pressed it into Makoto's hand.

A small patch. Embroidered with the motto of the pararescuemen.

"That Ot

kadena.t: 🇺🇸 His guns froze... So he brought down a Japanese aircraft with his Corsair’s propeller. Then he flew home! May 10, 1945. Above Okinawa, four Marine Corsairs…
kadena.tx:
🇺🇸 His guns froze... So he brought down a Japanese aircraft with his Corsair’s propeller. Then he flew home!

May 10, 1945. Above Okinawa, four Marine Corsairs climbed after a Japanese reconnaissance aircraft.

Two couldn’t climb any farther. Captain Kenneth Reusser and his wingman, First Lieutenant Robert R. Klingman of VMF-312, kept going.

They even fired off ammunition to lighten their aircraft.

At roughly 38,000 feet, Reusser got within range. He hit the Japanese aircraft, then exhausted his remaining ammunition.

Klingman moved in to finish the attack.

He pressed the trigger.

Nothing.

According to the Marine Corps’ official history, the cold had frozen his guns. The enemy aircraft was still flying, and its rear gunner was still a threat.

Klingman closed in until his Corsair’s spinning propeller struck the Japanese aircraft’s tail.

One attack wasn’t enough. He came back.

Accounts describe three passes before he had cut away enough of the tail surfaces to send the aircraft plunging toward the sea.

That’s a whole different level of badass. But this tough guy still had to get home!

His Corsair had taken bullets. Its propeller and engine cowling were battered. Pieces of the Japanese aircraft were lodged in his own.

Yet he reached Kadena and landed without injury.

A photograph taken afterward shows him examining the damaged propeller—the part that had kept his fighter airborne and become his weapon.

Klingman received the Navy Cross. His citation explicitly credits him with destroying the enemy aircraft by severing its tail surfaces with his propeller.

The damage was photographed. The action was recorded. And the pilot lived to tell the story.

For more WWII stories, follow @Vanguard_WW2 

📷 USMC: Robert R. Klingman inspecting his damaged Corsair propeller at Kadena, May 10, 1945.

Tucker Carlson reports that Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing Donald Trump to launch a nuclear strike on Iran. Before that idea gains any ground in Washington, its consequences need to be understood. More than 180 countries renounced nuclear weapons under a set of explicit promises. A nuclear attack on Iran would show those promises to be worthless.

The bargain is written into the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty itself. Under Article II, non-nuclear-weapon states agreed not to acquire nuclear arms. In return, they were promised three things: the inalienable right to peaceful nuclear energy, good-faith negotiations toward disarmament by the nuclear powers, and - when the treaty was extended indefinitely - assurances that nuclear weapons would not be used against them, noted by the Security Council in Resolution 984. In Iran’s case, the first promise has already been broken: its peaceful programme has been sanctioned and bombed. The second has gone unmet for decades. A nuclear strike would break the third.

The regime urging this strike has never accepted any part of that bargain. Israel refuses to join the NPT, has never acknowledged the arsenal it built at Dimona, and has ignored Security Council Resolution 487 calling on it to place its nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards. When Mordechai Vanunu exposed the programme, Israeli agents abducted him in Rome and he spent 18 years in prison. Under the Begin Doctrine, Israel claims the right to bomb any state in the region it suspects of seeking the capability it already possesses, while demanding total transparency from its neighbours and accepting none for itself. At the same time, Israel stands accused of genocide and of widespread war crimes and crimes against humanity. Its forces have repeatedly violated the sovereignty of neighbouring states through cross-border strikes and occupations, and it has pursued an openly aggressive posture across the region. Its prime minister is wanted by the International Criminal Court. This is the war criminal now urging Washington to use the most destructive weapon ever built against a member of the treaty his regime has spent half a century evading.

Iran’s record points the other way. It negotiated the JCPOA, which the Security Council endorsed unanimously in Resolution 2231, and the IAEA confirmed its compliance in report after report. Washington walked away anyway. When Iran returned to the table, it was attacked twice: days before a scheduled round with U.S. envoys, and hours after talks in Geneva that Oman’s foreign minister said had brought the two sides close to a genuine agreement.

Article X allows any party to withdraw if extraordinary events related to the treaty have jeopardised its supreme interests. A nuclear attack on a member that negotiated, complied, and kept returning to diplomacy would hand that argument to every other member. Islamic countries will rightly see an ethno-supremacist and racist ideology behind this use of nuclear weapons. A nuclear strike against a Muslim-majority nation, urged by a regime that has long defined itself in ethno-religious terms and that has never accepted the restraints of the NPT, would be read not as a narrow security measure but as the expression of a deeper hierarchy of peoples. That perception would further erode confidence in the treaty among its Islamic members and accelerate momentum toward withdrawal. The treaty rests on a single premise: that a state can give up the bomb and still be safe. If that premise fails in Iran, parliaments, politicians, and publics across the membership will start asking whether staying in serves their security. Some governments will decide that it does not. Withdrawals, individual or collective, would follow, and the non-proliferation regime would simply not survive them.

fordow.t: Trump is reportedly contemplating using nuclear weapons against Iran's facilities. This is exactly and precisely where all those who advocated withdrawing from…
fordow.tx:
Trump is reportedly contemplating using nuclear weapons against Iran's facilities. This is exactly and precisely where all those who advocated withdrawing from the JCPOA, and then "maximum pressure," wanted him to be.

Trace the timeline. First, they claimed the JCPOA was a bad deal that needed fixing. Remember the Foundation for Defense of Democracies' motto, "fix it or nix it"? Then they lured him out of the agreement by insisting it could not be fixed. Then they lobbied for the most extreme economic measures imaginable under maximum pressure. Then the narrative quietly shifted: economic pressure alone would not work, they said, and diplomacy with Iran required a "credible threat of military force." Just short of calling for war.

Once the use of force was normalized, they set about getting him to actually use it. Report after report argued that designating Iran's official armed forces, the IRGC, as a terrorist organization, and then assassinating Iran's top general, would make Tehran cave. It didn't. But the ice had been broken. From then on, every step was an escalation, and every diplomatic initiative that might have eased tensions or produced a peaceful settlement was attacked and buried.

Then came the strike on Fordow, alongside Israel. Then the war in February, in which they got him to cross every red line and pushed a settlement further out of reach than ever.

Running in parallel all these years was a campaign to persuade Washington that diplomacy with Iran is a waste of time and that the only option worth keeping on the table is the military one. Iran is just "buying time," they said. Iran never honors its commitments, they said, even as IAEA inspectors verified its compliance over and over. You can't negotiate with the world's leading state sponsor of terrorism. Iran cannot be trusted. Iran is weak. Why bother negotiate with a “significantly weakened Iran” when you can simply use force to extract concessions?

So much for "weak"!

Every one of these assumptions has proved false. Yet instead of asking why they were wrong at every turn, they read each failure as proof that the last measure was too mild. 

And so here we are. Openly discussing war crimes, threatening to wipe out power plants and bridges, bombing civilian infrastructure and even weighing nuclear weapons have all become ordinary instruments of policy. 

They took a president who brandished "The Art of the Deal" and sold himself as the ultimate dealmaker, and turned him into a man deciding whether to become the first leader since Truman to use a nuclear weapon. Against whom? A country that was already at the negotiating table, prepared to reach an equitable agreement.

So don't let them ever claim this was about a bad nuclear deal that needed correcting. It was always about Israel's destructive agenda, carried into Washington by its lobbies, its mouthpieces and its PR firms.

There is an old fable about a frog dropped into a pot of water that is heated so slowly it never thinks to jump. Each degree feels bearable, because it is only one degree warmer than the last. The frog never notices the moment the water starts to boil. Washington is that frog. And the water is already boiling.

fordow.tx:
🇮🇷|Araghchi to Merz: "There Will Be No More Red Lines." Germany's Welcome of the Airstrikes Has Been Noted. And So Has Its Bill.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X on Saturday, 31 October 2026: "When U.S. and Zionist airstrikes against Iran began last year, Mr. Merz welcomed these attacks, describing them as the execution of 'Europe's dirty work.'"

Then the line that matters: "A sum of 100 billion euros cannot be compared to the decisive and devastating response that the Iranian armed forces will deliver to anyone who dares to violate our nation's sovereignty; there will be no more 'red lines.'"

The Foreign Minister named the co-belligerent.

Friedrich Merz is not an observer. He is the German Chancellor. When US and Israeli aircraft bombed Natanz, Fordow, and Isfahan in June 2025, Merz did not call for restraint. He welcomed the strikes. He called them Europe's dirty work, a phrasing that admits the continent wanted the bombing done and preferred that someone else's pilots do it. Araghchi has now put that admission on the record from the Iranian foreign ministry's own account.

That is not a diplomatic exchange. That is a charge sheet.

Read what "no more red lines" means.

For two decades Iran operated inside a restraint doctrine. It stayed in the NPT. It accepted IAEA inspections. It negotiated the JCPOA. It absorbed the US withdrawal from that deal in 2018. It absorbed the assassination of its scientists. It absorbed the bombing of its safeguarded facilities and the IAEA's silence about who dropped the bombs. Every stage of that restraint was a red line Iran chose not to cross.

Araghchi has just announced the end of that doctrine. "No more red lines" is not a threat aimed at one country. It is the formal abandonment of the restraint architecture. It tells Berlin, Washington, and Tel Aviv that the calculation that kept Iran inside limits no longer applies.

The 100 billion euros is the German rearmament bill, and Araghchi sized it against the wrong column.

The 100 billion euro figure is the German defence fund Berlin created to rebuild the Bundeswehr. Araghchi compared it to the response the Iranian armed forces will deliver. His point is arithmetic, not rhetoric: money buys hardware, and hardware does not answer what Iran answers with. German defence procurement is a budget line. Iranian retaliation is a doctrine that has already been demonstrated against Saudi airports at Najran, Khamis Mushait, and Abha.

The deeper layer Berlin does not want examined.

Germany presents itself as a diplomatic actor in the Iran file. It was an E3 member of the JCPOA negotiations. It signed the deal. Then it stood with Washington after Washington destroyed the deal. Then it welcomed the bombing campaign that hit the facilities the deal had verified.

Berlin supplied the political cover. The United States and Israel supplied the aircraft. Merz called it Europe's dirty work because he understood the division of labour. Germany wanted the Iranian nuclear programme bombed without German aircraft in the sky and without German crews in the cockpits. It got what it wanted and then told its public it was a spectator.

Araghchi has refused the spectator framing. He has put Merz in the co-belligerent column, by name, from the foreign ministry's official account.

The contradiction Washington and Berlin cannot resolve.

Germany is not an NPT nuclear weapons state. It shelters under NATO's nuclear umbrella. It hosts US nuclear weapons at Büchel. It lectures Iran about NPT compliance while sitting inside a nuclear sharing arrangement. It welcomed the bombing of safeguarded facilities inside a non-nuclear-weapons state that was, at the moment of the bombing, under IAEA inspection.

The IAEA withdrew its inspectors from Iran in June 2025 because of the safety risk of the strikes. The Security Council has since drafted resolutions blaming Iran for the resulting loss of continuity. Germany voted for the architecture that produced that outcome

A detailed analysis using historical November wind data (Japan Meteorological Agency) for a 360 kt surface burst finds that the 
dominant wind direction is eastward over Iran’s central desert toward Afghanistan on 68% of days (average 19 m/s from the west). Never toward Tehran, Qom, or Iraq in the last 10 Novembers.

Dangerous fallout stays largely local and within Iran. Lethal doses (450+ rem) and radiation sickness doses (100+ rem) do not extend beyond Iran in the model. The plume fades below 1 rem beyond Herat in western Afghanistan.

Pakistan & India: No meaningful dose. Highest modeled dose anywhere in India is 0.5 rem (most days far lower). Natural background radiation is already 0.25 rem/year. Distance to Indian territory is 1,860 km; Karachi, Islamabad, New Delhi, and Mumbai are well outside significant fallout range.
Casualties: Mostly from the blast itself near Natanz (3,500 on a typical day up to 11,000 on calm days when fallout settles nearby). Sheltering indoors would cut radiation casualties substantially.

Important caveats
This assumes a single nuclear surface burst. A conventional strike (even with bunker busters) would not produce this kind of radioactive fallout plume at all, only local dust, possible uranium contamination if material is present, and debris.

Real outcomes depend heavily on exact yield, burst height, and the specific weather on the day, of course, the political and geostrategic impact thay would be felt globally.

After reading @TuckerCarlson’s post below, felt like searching on Google: What are the dangers of nuking a country such as Iran? Below was google’s response: 

A nuclear attack—whether an actual detonation of a nuclear weapon or a catastrophic strike on a nuclear facility (such as the Bushehr reactor or enrichment sites like Natanz and Fordo in a country like Iran)—carries catastrophic, multi-layered dangers: 

1. Immediate Physical and Health Destruction
•Vaporization, Blast, and Thermal Waves: An actual nuclear detonation causes instant vaporization near ground zero, massive blast waves that shatter buildings, and intense thermal heat triggering giant firestorms. 
•Mass Casualties & Collapse of Healthcare: Tens of millions or millions of people would face immediate death or severe burns, trauma, and radiation sickness. Remaining medical infrastructure, hospitals, and pharmacies would be rapidly overwhelmed or destroyed. 

2. Radiological Release and Environmental Contamination
•Attacks on Nuclear Reactors or Enrichment Sites: Hitting a nuclear power plant (like Bushehr) or spent fuel ponds can breach containment, releasing dangerous radioactive isotopes—such as Iodine-131, Cesium-137, and Polonium-210—into the air and water. 
•Regional Water and Desalination Crises: In a region like the Persian Gulf, radioactive contamination of seawater threatens vital desalination plants in neighboring countries (such as Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, and Saudi Arabia), potentially cutting off drinking water supplies within days. 
•Fallout and Air Currents: Radioactive clouds can cross national borders, matching or recalling historical cross-border contamination events like Chernobyl. 

3. Long-Term Health and Genetic Consequences
•Radiation Illness & Cancers: Survivors experience acute radiation syndrome (hair loss, internal bleeding, immune system collapse) followed decades later by high rates of radiation-induced cancers (such as thyroid cancer) and increased risks of birth abnormalities or leukemia in future generations. 
•Food & Famine Risks: Widespread soil and water contamination, combined with the collapse of local agriculture and distribution networks, risk mass starvation and severe malnutrition. 

4. Global and Regional Geopolitical Fallout
•Regional Escalation and Arms Races: A strike on or by a nation like Iran risks immediate retaliatory spirals, drawing in regional and global powers, destabilizing the Middle East, and unraveling international non-proliferation treaties. 
•Global Climate Disruption: Large-scale nuclear exchanges or massive fires inject millions of tons of soot into the upper atmosphere, potentially causing global cooling ("nuclear winter") and global agricultural failure.

parchin.t: An Islamic Republic official admits the regime lied about the massive damage inflicted by U.S. and Israeli strikes, blaming explosions at military sites on nat…
parchin.tx:
An Islamic Republic official admits the regime lied about the massive damage inflicted by U.S. and Israeli strikes, blaming explosions at military sites on natural events such as thunder and lightning.

Mohammad Sadegh Koushki, a hardline regime figure appearing on state television, described the deception openly. Israeli strikes on the Kermanshah drone base were publicly blamed on thunder and lightning, while repeated attacks on missile facilities and other sensitive military sites were never announced.

This was not an isolated cover story. It was part of a systematic campaign to hide the scale of the regime’s military losses while exaggerating its remaining strength and supposed victories.

“Gas leaks” are another standard cover story used when explosions occur at or near sensitive military, missile and IRGC-linked facilities. Like the lightning excuse, the explanation allows the regime to disguise a possible attack or act of sabotage as an ordinary domestic accident.

In June 2020, a massive nighttime explosion near the Parchin military complex was officially blamed on a gas leak at a storage facility in a public area. Satellite imagery later revealed extensive damage and scorch marks at the adjacent Khojir missile-production complex, directing attention toward a facility associated with missile propellants rather than the harmless location described by the regime.

The same pattern resurfaced after the July 2025 explosion at the Pamchal 9 complex, a residential building connected to the Armed Forces Judicial Organization. State and judiciary media blamed owner negligence and a gas leak. Residents reportedly disputed the explanation, saying the building was not connected to the municipal gas network and that the damage across several floors did not resemble an ordinary domestic explosion.

Other explosions near military and industrial facilities have been attributed to gas leaks, aging infrastructure or routine accidents. In some cases, regime-linked outlets initially raised the possibility of Israeli involvement before deleting those references and adopting the official accident narrative.

When U.S. and Israeli strikes damaged drone bases, missile-production facilities, air defences, naval assets and command centres, the regime responded with silence, weather excuses and restrictions on reporting from the affected areas. Evidence of destruction was concealed from Iranians because acknowledging it would expose the failure of the military system that consumed enormous national resources while proving unable to protect itself.

The regime simultaneously manufactured stories of overwhelming retaliation. State television and IRGC-linked outlets claimed Iranian missiles had destroyed strategic Israeli sites, devastated American forces and achieved extraordinary success rates. Many of these claims relied on recycled footage, manipulated imagery, fabricated casualty figures or targets that independent evidence showed remained operational.

The strategy was simple. Hide Iranian losses, invent enemy losses and preserve the illusion that the regime remained in control.

The actual damage was substantial, although American assessments differed over its permanence. U.S. Central Command described severe degradation across Iran’s missile, drone, naval and defence-industrial infrastructure. It reported that launch rates had fallen dramatically and that large portions of production capacity and major naval assets had been destroyed.

More cautious American intelligence assessments concluded that Iran retained significant missile stocks, mobile launchers and access to many underground facilities. That means the regime was badly damaged but not disarmed. It still possesses dangerous capabilities and could rebuild parts of its arsenal over time.

Both assessments, however, contradict the Islamic Republic’s claim that its forces emerged largely intact or even stronger.

Even hardline critics of the Iranian government also wrote articles, launched a petition and rallied in Toronto on Sunday against Canada’s position. Some of the opponents of the Islamic Republic pointed out that Ottawa didn’t publish any legal explanation for its support of UAE’s territorial claims over islands Iran has formally controlled since just before UAE’s 1971 creation and prior to the Islamic Republic.

As Ottawa has put Iran’s territorial integrity into question, it has also portrayed a country bombed tens of thousands of times recently as an aggressor. A number of reports linked to Canada’s new National Security Strategy suggested Iran has been attacking Canada (in reality, Ottawa has severed relations, labeled Iran a state sponsor of terror, listed part of its army a terror group, seized its diplomatic assets and imposed dozens of rounds of sanctions in support of a long-standing Zionist/imperial campaign against Iran).

On Tuesday CBC published “Why a spate of gun-for-hire shootings in Toronto were likely paid for by Iran. Attacks on Jewish, U.S. and anti-regime targets fit worldwide pattern of violence.” Despite the bold headline, there’s no evidence presented in the article linking Iran to the shootings. In a complaint to the CBC, Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East’s Media Accountability Project noted, “What is not established through the facts in the article is any concrete link to Iran.” (Does anyone believe Tehran benefits to the point of paying random individuals shooting up various institutions in Toronto?)

Politically the CBC story served its purposes. In response, Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre reiterated his call to deport Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) operatives and the claims also boosted the anti-Iran angle in coverage of Canada’s new National Security Strategy.
Two days later the front of the Globe and Mail read: “Officials flag unprecedented security threats against Jewish community.” The third paragraph of an article tied to the release of the National Security Strategy mentioned “threats from Iran”. In another story this week, CSIS officials reportedly told Iran International they had “disrupted potentially lethal threats against people in Canada in multiple cases involving Iranian intelligence or proxies.”

Concurrently, Liberal MPs Anthony Housefather and Judy Sgro told the House of Commons Iran was a threat and criminal. Housefather announced a parliamentary petition calling the Iranian government a danger to Canadians while Sgro spoke “in solidarity with the courageous people and political prisoners of Iran” and “the ‘no to execution Tuesdays’ campaign.”

🩺 Care That Reaches Every Community

Reaffirming its commitment to community welfare and humanitarian assistance, the INDBATT Medical Team conducted a Medical Assistance Camp at Kafer Chouba , extending essential healthcare services to the local population within its Area of Responsibility.

The camp provided medical consultations, treatment and necessary medicines to residents, with particular attention to those facing challenges in accessing regular healthcare facilities. Through these services, the team addressed immediate medical needs while contributing to better health and well-being within the community.

The positive response from local residents reflected the importance of such outreach initiatives. Beyond medical assistance, the camp provided an opportunity for meaningful engagement and demonstrated INDBATT’s continued solidarity with the people of Kafer Chouba, further strengthening civil-military cooperation, mutual trust and goodwill.

Through consistent humanitarian outreach, INDBATT remains committed to supporting local communities and nurturing lasting bonds of friendship and cooperation across South Lebanon.

Extending care. Building trust. Strengthening community bonds. 🩺🤝🇱🇧🇺🇳🇮🇳

Its fighters have reportedly taken the entire Al-Maqatirah district in Lahj province, and on Monday were battling government forces at a military camp at the entrance to Tur al-Bahah district, one of the main approaches to Aden.

In the last 72 hours, Ansarallah has captured the highlands of the historic Al-Maqaterah District in Lahij Governorate after seizing control of Al-Maqaterah Castle. 

Forces from Al-Maqaterah District then traveled southwest to meet up with Ansar forces in Al Madaribah and Ras Al Ara District as they advanced along multiple fronts extending down to Jabal Al Rafad and the village of Ad Durad.

Only a couple hundred square kilometers of highland terrain remains under the control of the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council (PLC) in the vicinity of the Bab Al-Mandab.

bab-al-mandab.tx:
💢🇾🇪 UPDATE: Ansarallah forces have taken the al-Maqatirah district administration building and the district's hilltop fortress in Yemen's southern Lahj province, bringing them within 5 kilometers (~3 miles) of the center of neighboring Tur al-Baha, according to a Yemeni commentator aligned with the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council. 

Saudi outlets claim the Giants Brigades, a UAE-built force, and Saudi Arabia's Homeland Shield forces, both fighting for the council, have instead retaken positions and contained the advance. Drop Site could not independently confirm either account.

The push threatens to encircle the council's forces in the coastal pocket they hold at the Bab al-Mandab Strait. With Ansarallah already controlling the high ground to the north and the Red Sea coast to the west, taking Tur al-Baha and pushing south on the main road from Taiz to Aden would sever the routes that link the pocket to Aden, the council's base and the main source of its reinforcements and supplies. 

Sharing the report, Ansarallah-aligned commentator Hussain al-Bukhaiti suggested Ansarallah could soon capture Ras al-Ara port on the Gulf of Aden, comparing it to Ansarallah's rapid seizure of the Red Sea port of Mocha on Sept. 10. Taking Ras al-Ara would put Ansarallah on both sides of the strait.

suez.t: Oct 31, 1956. An Egyptian warship sails in alone to bombard an Israeli city. By breakfast, she has a new flag and a new name. Ibrahim el Awal had a long histor…
suez.tx:
Oct 31, 1956. An Egyptian warship sails in alone to bombard an Israeli city. By breakfast, she has a new flag and a new name.

Ibrahim el Awal had a long history before that night. She was built as HMS Mendip, a British destroyer that fought in World War II. Later she was loaned to Nationalist China, then sold to Egypt.

On Oct 29, 1956, Israel invaded the Sinai, the start of the Suez Crisis. The next night, Egypt sent Ibrahim el Awal alone toward Haifa, Israel's main port, to shell its oil installations.

At about 3:30 a.m. on Oct 31, she opened fire. Over the next 20 minutes or so she fired around 200 shells at the city. They did little damage and killed no one.

Anchored in Haifa harbor was a French destroyer, Kersaint, part of the secret British and French plan to retake the Suez Canal. She fired back. No hits, but the Egyptian ship turned and ran northwest.

Two Israeli destroyers, Eilat and Yafo, went after her. The chase went on for hours. The Israeli ships fired hundreds of rounds, but their gunners were inexperienced and scored few hits.

At dawn, two Israeli Air Force Ouragan jets arrived and hit her with rockets, knocking out her generator and rudder. Dead in the water, Ibrahim el Awal surrendered just after 7 a.m. Two of her crew had been killed and eight wounded.

Her crew tried to scuttle her. The valves were rusted shut.

Eilat towed her into Haifa, the city she had just shelled. About 200 Egyptian sailors were taken prisoner.

The Israeli Navy repaired her and commissioned her as INS Haifa.

There's a grim twist. The destroyer Eilat, which towed her in, was sunk by Egyptian missiles in 1967, the first ship ever sunk by ship-launched missiles.

Too suspicious to ignore! @NavalWarCollege/@ChinaMaritime Note 26—“Easy Infiltration: The Rise of PRC Small Boat Landings on Taiwan”

From CMSI Director CAPT @ChrisHSharman, @USNavy (Ret.)—

#China-#Taiwan Watchers:

Could seemingly isolated small-boat landings on Taiwan be something more than cases of illegal entry?

Beginning in 2021, at least 8 PRC nationals have been arrested after making small-boat crossings of the Taiwan Strait & landing on Taiwan.

Each reported landing occurred at a sensitive location. 5/8 occurred on known invasion beaches; the other 3 were at ports & river deltas believed to be of high interest to PLA war planners.

In CMSI Note #26, “Easy Infiltration: The Rise of PRC Small Boat Landings on Taiwan,” CMSI’s Professor @Ian_M_Easton meticulously documents these incidents & examines their potential security implications.

Professor Easton begins by exploring what PLA textbooks say about infiltrating undercover operatives into Taiwan to conduct reconnaissance & special missions, placing these activities in the context of PLA amphibious invasion planning.

Professor Easton is careful to note that there is no public evidence establishing that the individuals involved were PLA operatives.
There are, however, reasons to question whether these incidents are entirely unrelated or innocuous.

He examines several possible explanations, including smuggling, espionage, & reconnaissance, ultimately arguing that PLA involvement cannot be ruled out.

This CMSI Note also offers practical recommendations for strengthening Taiwan’s defenses against potential infiltration, including improved coastal surveillance, coast-watcher communities, & the fortification of vulnerable beaches & coastal garrisons.

Richly illustrated with photographs, maps, & media accounts documenting the individual incidents, this note provides a fascinating look at an emerging & potentially consequential dimension of Taiwan’s coastal security challenges.

In Beledweyne, Macawisley fighters took parts of the Lama-Galay compound and its administration offices on 30 October, amid a dispute over the Hirshabelle governorship.

At the UN Security Council, the US draft on Western Sahara won 11 votes but was vetoed by Russia, with China, Pakistan and Somalia abstaining. Russia's own text won only 3 votes, one of them Somalia's.
